metadata.title: Do 15-year-olds know how to manage money? (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief summarizes results from the PISA 2012 financial literacy assessment using the OECD PISA 2012 Database. The document does not report the specific student sampling/replicate weight variables or whether complex-survey variance estimation was applied in the computations shown. For analysts working with PISA microdata, the recommended approach is to use the provided student sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) to account for the stratified, clustered sampling design and the multistage selection of students and schools. The brief also does not describe any additional preprocessing beyond using the published PISA 2012 database tables, so weight application should follow the standard PISA analysis procedures for the relevant derived scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive policy brief summarizing published PISA 2012 financial literacy results rather than reporting an original student-level predictive model with an explicit PV-based outcome. Because no PV estimation procedure or missing-data strategy is described for an ML/empirical modeling pipeline, the PV and missing-data handling details are not applicable to the extraction target here. The brief relies on OECD’s already-produced PISA 2012 database outputs (e.g., mean scores and proficiency-level shares), so the underlying PV/missing-data processing is not documented in this text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief states that PISA 2012 included a financial literacy assessment with participation by about 29,000 students across 18 OECD and partner countries and economies. It does not specify any additional analytic filtering (e.g., grade subsamples, exclusions, or task-completion criteria) beyond using the OECD PISA 2012 Database tables referenced in the text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief reports descriptive results from PISA 2012’s first international financial literacy assessment. Across 13 participating OECD countries and economies, 10% of students can analyse complex financial products and solve non-routine problems, while 15% can at best make simple everyday spending decisions and recognise everyday financial documents such as invoices. Proficiency varies substantially: Shanghai-China has the highest mean score (603), and the gap between the highest- and lowest-performing countries/economies exceeds 225 points overall, with 75 score points (about one proficiency level) separating the top and bottom among OECD countries. Only 16% of between-country differences in mean financial literacy are explained by country wealth. The brief also highlights that financial literacy is distinct from mathematics and reading, and that gender differences are small on average but can favour boys among students with comparable math and reading performance in many systems.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an original empirical ML paper: it is a descriptive OECD policy brief summarizing already-published PISA 2012 financial literacy results (means, proficiency-level shares, and relative performance comparisons). As a result, there is no student-level predictive modeling pipeline to extract (no ML algorithms, no PV-handling procedure, no missing-data strategy, and no reported model performance metrics). The sparse methodological fields reflect the document’s purpose as a dissemination product rather than a methods-and-results research article.
